tagline.text: The Philippines' first women's museum, honoring the Mother of the Revolution

location.label: Location
location.text: Banlat Road, Barangay Tandang Sora, Quezon City (beside the Tandang Sora National Shrine)

children.text: Opened in 2025 by Quezon City, this is billed as the first women's museum in the Philippines. It stands right beside the national shrine to Tandang Sora (Melchora Aquino), the Mother of the Revolution, and its two-story bahay na bato–style building traces the history of women from the babaylan to the modern women's movement.

The Tandang Sora Women's Museum was built by the Quezon City government, which presents it as the first women's museum in the Philippines. It stands on Banlat Road in Barangay Tandang Sora, Quezon City, right next to the Tandang Sora National Shrine. It had a soft opening on
January 6
, 2025, Tandang Sora's 213th birthday, and was formally inaugurated on
February 19

, which is also the day she died. According to the city government, the exhibits consist of a Tandang Sora section, a creativity corner, an audio-visual space, a rotating art exhibit, and a timeline. Admission was free to everyone in February and March 2025, and a set fee applies afterward.

Melchora Aquino (1812–1919) is commonly known as Tandang Sora, or "Old Sora." In August 1896, when Katipunan members (the secret society fighting Spanish colonial rule) were being hunted, she opened her home and store to them and gave them food, medical care, and advice. She was arrested for it and held in Bilibid Prison in Manila, where she refused to talk under interrogation, and that
September 2
she was ordered deported to the Mariana Islands (Guam). That is how she earned the titles
Mother of the Revolution
and
Mother of Balintawak

. She was born on January 6, 1812, in Banlat, then part of Caloocan (now the Tandang Sora area of Quezon City), and died on February 19, 1919, at the age of 107. She was already elderly during the revolution, which is how she got the name "Tandang" (old), and her profile appeared on the five-centavo coin used from 1967 to 1994.

The building was designed by a team led by architect Gerard Lico, and its two stories draw on the bahay na bato, the traditional Philippine house with a stone ground floor and a wooden upper floor. The exhibits were developed by feminist artist Sandra Torrijos as curator. The museum is not just a memorial to one person; it aims to bring together the roles Filipino women have played in faith, politics, peacebuilding, revolution, the arts, science, and the media.
It is not large, and 1–2 hours is plenty even at a relaxed pace. Many visitors pair it with the bronze statue, about

tall, and the small gallery at the neighboring national shrine on the same grounds, then continue to Quezon Memorial Circle or La Mesa Ecopark for a half-day trip. Please check the latest opening hours and fees with the Quezon City tourism office before you go. The museum is compact, so there is no need to rush, and it is easy with young children. Even without background knowledge, you can follow the exhibits by reading the captions slowly.

This section introduces the life of Melchora Aquino and her role in the revolution. Items such as the kitchen utensils she used and other materials are on display, letting you feel the everyday life of a figure about whom few records survive. It is also meaningful that the formal opening date is the anniversary of her death.

This is the museum's flagship exhibit, showing in chronological order the roles women have played in faith, leadership, peacebuilding, revolution, and culture, from the babaylan (women spiritual leaders) of ancient times to women in today's politics, arts, science, and media. It also covers women-led labor unions. It is on the second floor, so take your time reading as you go up.

This is an interactive space on the ground floor. Using visual art, archival photos, and multimedia, it shows the role of Filipino women in the struggle for independence and spotlights women whose stories are often left out of standard history books.

This area gathers materials from various feminist movements. Items such as a pis syabit, a traditional Tausug head covering from Jolo, Sulu, have been reported on display, and there is also a "Sino Sila" ("Who are they") exhibit introducing women across generations.
There is a space where you can learn through video and sound, plus books on the history of Filipino women to read. This makes the visit less dull than a museum where you only walk and read.
The two-story building is an attraction in itself. Its exterior, inspired by traditional Philippine houses, is good for photos, and ramps and a lift make it fairly easy to get around.

The shrine next door was built in 2008 and declared a national shrine by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines in 2012. Her remains are kept in a niche beneath the bronze statue, about
tall.

blocks.title: Gallery and open-air stage in the shrine

children.text: The shrine grounds include a gallery of works by Quezon City artists and a pavilion and stage for events. It is easy to visit them together with the museum in one trip.
Arrive when the museum opens and buy your ticket. If you are not a Quezon City resident, have
ready, and bring plenty of cash in case you have no resident ID.
Start with the Tandang Sora tribute space on the ground floor. Seeing items such as her kitchen utensils first gives you the background to understand the exhibits that follow.
On the ground floor, see the Isip at Gawa creativity corner, the audio-visual space, and the rotating art exhibit.
Go up to the second floor and walk along the HERstorical Philippine Timeline. Read it in chronological order from the babaylan to modern women, and allow about
30 minutes
See the Women in Action and Sino Sila exhibits, then rest for a moment at the book corner.
Cross to the neighboring national shrine to see the bronze statue, the niche, and the gallery inside the shrine.
Have lunch at a nearby restaurant. There is no confirmed information about a restaurant inside the museum, so it is safer to eat outside.

The museum closes early in the afternoon, so rather than going back in after lunch, plan to finish in the morning. It is closed on Mondays, so go from Tuesday to Sunday. If you use a wheelchair or stroller, ask at the entrance where the lift is.
Spend about
2 hours
at the museum and shrine.
After lunch, take a taxi or Grab to Quezon Memorial Circle. It is about
4km
in a straight line, and the travel time varies greatly with traffic.
Walk around
Quezon Memorial Circle
If you have time, continue to
La Mesa Ecopark
. Check its admission hours locally.
Weekday afternoon traffic in Quezon City is heavy, so allow plenty of travel time.
From Manila (MNL) airport or central Manila, a taxi or Grab is the simplest option. Tell the driver "Tandang Sora National Shrine, Banlat Road, Quezon City."
It is about
20km
from the airport and can take
1 hour
or more depending on traffic.
Jeepneys and UV Express vans run along Tandang Sora Avenue, but I could not confirm the current routes and stops, so ask locally.
In a map app, search for "Tandang Sora Women's Museum" to find the location.
Within Quezon City, Grab is convenient, and tricycles work for short distances.
The museum and the national shrine are next door to each other, so you can walk between them.
If you cannot get a Grab on the way back, walk out to the main road, Tandang Sora Avenue, and book from there.
The exhibits are mostly indoors, so you can visit even on a rainy day. Still, considering the shrine's outdoor areas and travel time, the dry season from December to May is more comfortable.

Commemorative events are often held around Tandang Sora's birthday (January 6) and the anniversary of her death (February 19), and during National Arts Month in February and Women's Month in March. Admission was free in February and March 2025, but later rules may change, so check the latest announcements.

There is no cluster of accommodations around the museum, so the usual approach is to stay elsewhere in Quezon City or in central Manila and make a day trip. Quezon City is close to central Manila, so it is easy to fit into a one-day itinerary.

You will not eat inside the museum but at nearby restaurants or shops along the main road. I could not confirm whether the museum has a restaurant, so bring water and snacks. Local restaurants often change their opening hours. It also helps to decide in advance whether you want Korean or Filipino food for lunch after the morning visit, which cuts down on travel. A mall food court has predictable prices and is a safe choice for first-time visitors.
The museum is closed on Mondays. The official information says Tuesday to Sunday from
to
, but one page lists a closing time of
, so check before you go.
Quezon City residents get in free with a valid ID. Foreign travelers should have
ready in cash.
You can make inquiries to the Quezon City tourism office (phone +63 915 392 1044).
Reading a little about who Tandang Sora was before you go makes the tribute space and the timeline much more interesting.
The timeline exhibit is on the second floor. Ramps and a lift are provided, so the building is described as wheelchair accessible.
A lactation room is provided, so families with young children can visit comfortably.
Exhibits are rotated, so the 2025 lineup may have changed. If there is an exhibit you want to see, ask in advance.
After heavy rain the outdoor areas of the shrine can be wet, so wear shoes that do not slip.
Commemorative events may be held at the shrine on January 6 (birthday) and February 19 (anniversary), so avoid those dates if you do not want crowds or busy photos.
Some days bring school groups and families, so weekday mornings are better if you want a quiet visit.
Opening hours and admission may change, so check the latest announcements with the Quezon City tourism office before you go. There was a separate free period right after the opening.
The museum is closed on Mondays and closes early, so you may not get in if you arrive late in the afternoon.
Quezon City traffic is heavy at weekday rush hours. Allow plenty of time for the return trip.
When you book a Grab, enter the destination exactly as the shrine's name. It is easy to confuse with similarly named places.
I could not confirm the photography rules inside the museum. Ask the staff at the entrance, and do not touch the exhibits.
A large park in the heart of the city, about
4km
in a straight line from the museum. It is good for walks and photos. With its monument and wide walkways, it makes a good follow-up stop after the museum.
A nature park with forest and a lake, about
4–5km
in a straight line from the museum. Check its opening hours locally.
The shrine right next to the museum, with a bronze statue about
tall, a niche holding her remains, and a gallery.
